inputs.question: In low- and middle-income countries, do programmes meant to improve education for children and young people with disabilities work, and which kinds work best?
inputs.scope:
Covers: Interventions in low- and middle-income countries aimed at improving educational access, participation, retention or learning outcomes for children and young people with disabilities. Examples include teacher training, inclusive-school reforms, assistive devices, curriculum adaptation, community and parent programmes, financial support, and school infrastructure. The question asks whether these work and how the different types compare.
Out of scope:
- Effectiveness of disability-inclusive education programmes in high-income countries (Context, resources and systems differ substantially, and the question is restricted to low- and middle-income countries.)
- Whether inclusive schooling or special schooling is the right model as a matter of rights and principle (That is a normative and legal question under the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (CRPD, Article 24), not an empirical question about programme effects.)
- Health, rehabilitation or functional outcomes of disability interventions (e.g. surgery, therapy) that are not measured on education outcomes (The question concerns educational outcomes. Clinical effectiveness is a separate body of evidence.)
- How many children with disabilities are out of school, and how disability is measured (e.g. the Washington Group questions) (Prevalence and the size of the gap are context for the question, not evidence of programme effectiveness.)
- General education interventions for all disadvantaged children that do not report effects separately for children with disabilities (Those studies do not answer whether the programmes work for this group.)
